title: RDSP Basics
summary: GET THE DTC → OPEN THE ACCOUNT → COLLECT GRANT AND BOND
subtitle: At certain income levels, a contribution of $1,500 can attract $3,500 in government grants. More than double your money, immediately.

blocks.text: The Registered Disability Savings Plan pays more government money, per dollar you put in, than any other account in this course.
At some income levels, a $1,500 deposit can bring in $3,500 in government grants. That’s more than double your money before any investment growth.
Yet many eligible Canadians still don’t have one open. It isn’t a bad deal. Most people have never had it explained.
Open the door to the most generous savings account in Canada.
blocks.detail: For a family living with a disability, an RDSP can turn small deposits, or none at all, into thousands in government money.
blocks.extra: Section 04 explains why to open one even if you can’t save.

blocks.text: There’s one gate, and everything else follows from it: the person the plan is for must be approved for the Disability Tax Credit (DTC).
You apply with Form T2201, which a medical practitioner fills out to confirm a severe and long-lasting impairment. Without DTC approval, you can’t open an RDSP at all.
If someone in your family has a long-term impairment and nobody has ever applied for the DTC, that application is the first step. It unlocks far more than this one account.
Beyond that, the person must live in Canada, have a Social Insurance Number and be under 60 when the plan is opened.
What DTC approval unlocks

items.title: THE TAX CREDIT ITSELF
items.text: For 2026, the DTC amount is $10,341, which can cut federal tax by up to $1,448 a year.

items.title: THE CANADA DISABILITY BENEFIT
items.text: Adults aged 18 to 64 with the DTC can get up to $204.20 a month from July 2026 to June 2027, based on income. You must file a tax return to get it.

items.title: THE RDSP
items.text: The account in this lesson, with its grants and bonds.

items.title: MORE FOR CHILDREN
items.text: Families of a child with the DTC can also get the Child Disability Benefit, paid with the Canada Child Benefit.

items.title: “The Disability Tax Credit is only for people who can’t work at all.”
items.text: The test is whether an impairment is severe and long-lasting and markedly limits daily life, not whether someone has a job. Many people who work full-time qualify. First applications are often turned down when they lack detail, then approved on a second try with more specific medical information.

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: YOU DO NOT NEED TO BE A LEGAL GUARDIAN TO OPEN ONE

One more barrier worth clearing up. For an adult who may not be able to sign a contract, opening an RDSP once meant going to court for guardianship first, a slow and costly step. Since 2012, a qualifying family member (a parent, spouse, common-law partner or, since 2023, a brother or sister) can open the plan instead, as long as no one already has legal authority. This rule ends on December 31, 2026. A family member who opens a plan before then can generally stay the plan holder after 2026. If this applies to you, ask your bank about it now.
The RDSP has two separate federal programs attached, and they work differently. It’s worth keeping them straight.

The grant matches what you put in. The Canada Disability Savings Grant matches your deposits. For family incomes up to about $117,000 in 2026, it pays $3 for every $1 on the first $500, and $2 for every $1 on the next $1,000. That’s $3,500 of grant on a $1,500 deposit. Above that income, it matches $1 for $1 on the first $1,000. The lifetime grant limit is $70,000.

The bond needs nothing from you. The Canada Disability Savings Bond pays into the account based on family income alone, with no deposit needed. It pays up to $1,000 a year, to a lifetime limit of $20,000. For a lower-income family who can’t spare anything, just having the account open can be worth real money.

items.title: THE GRANT (CDSG)
items.text: Needs a deposit. Up to $3,500 a year and $70,000 in a lifetime. Paid until the end of the year the person turns 49.

items.title: THE BOND (CDSB)
items.text: Needs no deposit. Up to $1,000 a year and $20,000 in a lifetime, for lower incomes. Paid until the end of the year the person turns 49.

sections.title: Open the account, even if you can’t contribute

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: OPEN THE ACCOUNT, EVEN IF YOU CAN’T CONTRIBUTE

This is the main point to carry away from this lesson. The bond needs no deposit. If family income qualifies, the government pays in just because the account exists and the person is eligible. Families sometimes decide an RDSP isn’t for them because money is tight and regular deposits feel impossible. But that is exactly the situation the bond was built for. Choosing not to open the account because you can’t contribute is the one choice that guarantees getting nothing. Opening it costs nothing. Leaving it unopened can cost thousands.

sections.title: Missed years can often be caught up

blocks.text: Grant and bond entitlements carry forward for up to 10 years.

A family who qualifies now but didn’t open an account earlier may be able to claim money from past years. Each year can catch up to $10,500 of grant and $11,000 of bond. That’s why opening the account soon matters: every year that passes, the oldest entitlements move closer to expiring.
Your RDSP provider can tell you how much carried-forward grant and bond room is still available, and how much you would need to deposit to collect it.

items.title: “If we didn’t open an RDSP when the diagnosis happened, we’ve missed our chance.”
items.text: Entitlements carry forward for up to 10 years. A family opening an account today may be able to claim several years of missed grants and bonds. It’s often far from too late, but the window keeps moving, so acting sooner collects more.

sections.title: Taking money out: the rule to plan around

blocks.text: Money can be taken out for anything that benefits the person the plan is for. There’s no rule about what it must be spent on.

But there’s a holdback rule to understand before you plan any withdrawals. If you take money out within 10 years of receiving a grant or bond, some of that government money must be paid back: generally $3 for every $1 you withdraw, up to the total received in those 10 years.
This isn’t a reason to avoid an RDSP. It’s a reason to treat it as the long-term account it was built to be, and to plan withdrawals around that 10-year timeline. An adviser who knows RDSPs can help.
Getting started with an RDSP

items.title: The person is approved for the Disability Tax Credit, or we’ve started the application.
We’ve opened the account, even if we can’t contribute regularly right now.
We’ve checked whether family income qualifies for the bond, which needs no deposit.
We’ve asked our provider how much carried-forward grant and bond room is left.
We understand the 10-year holdback rule before planning any withdrawals.

blocks.text: The Alvarez family’s second conversation
paragraphs: Marisol and Luis Alvarez lived in Saskatoon with their son Mateo, who has cerebral palsy. Mateo had been approved for the Disability Tax Credit two years earlier, and a nurse at the clinic had mentioned an RDSP in passing.

They never opened one. Luis drove a delivery truck, Marisol worked part-time, and every dollar already had a job. An account that seemed to need regular deposits felt like it was meant for families with more breathing room than they had.

The next spring, a social worker at Mateo’s day program brought it up again. Had anyone explained the bond? Nobody had. Their income was low enough that the government would pay into the account even if they never put in a dollar.

Marisol hesitated. The bank appointment meant a day of unpaid time off, and she had heard about clawbacks and rules she didn’t understand. She could keep putting it off, or she could take the day. That night she and Luis looked at the numbers together and booked the appointment for the following week.

At the bank, the adviser checked the carry-forward rules. Because entitlements reach back up to 10 years, the bond payments from the years they had missed were still there to claim. The account opened with thousands of dollars from the government, and none of it came from their budget.

On the drive home, Mateo asked what they had been doing all day. Marisol told him they had opened a savings account in his name. “For me?” he asked. Luis smiled in the rear-view mirror. “For you. It’s been waiting.”

blocks.text: The RDSP pays more government money per dollar than any other account in this course. Disability Tax Credit approval is the gate, and everything follows from it. The grant matches deposits, but the bond needs no deposit, so open the account even if you can’t contribute. Entitlements carry forward up to 10 years, and withdrawals within 10 years of a grant or bond trigger repayment, so plan for the long term.
One appointment can unlock years of government money for someone you love.
blocks.detail: Opening an RDSP now, even with nothing to deposit, collects the bond and keeps older entitlements from expiring.
blocks.extra: Section 08 walks you through your own RDSP check.

items.title: If someone in your family has a long-term impairment and has never applied for the Disability Tax Credit, book an appointment to have Form T2201 filled out. It’s the gate to everything here.
If the DTC is already approved, open an RDSP, even with no deposit. The bond may pay in anyway.
Ask your RDSP provider how much carried-forward grant and bond room is available.

blocks.text: Worksheet: your RDSP check

items.title: RDSP
items.text: Registered Disability Savings Plan. A long-term savings account for someone approved for the Disability Tax Credit.

items.title: DTC
items.text: Disability Tax Credit. Approval for a severe and long-lasting impairment, applied for with Form T2201. Needed to open an RDSP.

items.title: CDSG
items.text: Canada Disability Savings Grant. Government matching on deposits, up to $3,500 a year.

items.title: CDSB
items.text: Canada Disability Savings Bond. Government money paid based on family income, with no deposit needed.

items.title: Holdback
items.text: The rule that some grants and bonds from the past 10 years must be paid back when money is taken out.

items.title: Carry-forward
items.text: Unused grant and bond money that can still be claimed for up to 10 years.
